title: PID: Fixing Everything
question: How do we kill the droop *and* stop the wiggle?

blocks.text: Remember Chapter 2? Our P controller left the drone **hanging below 2 m**, and no $K_p$ could fix it. Time to find out what can.

To hold the drone up, the motors must push $mg \approx 4.9$ N, forever. A P controller only pushes when there's an error: $\eff{T} = K_p\,\err{e}$. So to push 4.9 N it *needs* an error of $\err{e} = mg/K_p$. With $K_p$ = 20 N/m that's $\err e$ = 4.9/20 ≈ 24.5 cm, forever. The droop isn't a bug in our tuning. It's the price P charges for holding anything up.
So we need a part of the controller that can push 4.9 N **with zero error**. Something with a memory.
Since Chapter 8 the motors are real: they can push between 0 and 20 N, no more, and they can't pull down. The orange thrust curves will flatten out when they hit a limit.

sections.title: I: a pile of past error

blocks.text: Here's the idea. Keep a running total of the error, the **area under the error curve**, exactly the "accumulating area" from [Chapter 3](#/ch/3). Push in proportion to that pile:

While the drone is below 2 m, the error is positive and the pile keeps growing, so the push keeps growing. The pile only stops growing when the error is **exactly zero**. At that point it simply *stays*, holding whatever thrust it has built up. That's the memory June wanted.
Oh, that's sneaky. The drone can't settle *anywhere* except 2 m, because anywhere else the pile would still be changing.

Stuck 24.5 cm low, the pile grows by 0.245 m·s every second. With $K_i$ = {scrub|ki|eff} N/(m·s) that adds {calc|rate|eff} N of push per second: at that pace, the whole 4.9 N would be there after {calc|tau} s. It never goes quite that fast. As the drone rises, the error shrinks and the pile slows down. After {calc|tau} s it's about 63% of the way; after about {calc|ts} s, 98%.
Hang on. 63% after one time constant? That's the coffee from Chapter 3!
Because it *is* the coffee. Once the fast wiggle is gone, P pushes whatever the pile doesn't. So the error is the missing push divided by $K_p$, and the pile grows by that error.
It grows in proportion to how far it still has to go. Chapter 3!

So the droop dies like cooling coffee, with a time constant of about $K_p/K_i$ = 2 s at our gains. On Chapter 8's map that's a slow pole near $-K_i/K_p = -0.5$. (Only "about": the fast wiggle needs a moment to fade, and with a big $K_i$ the two get mixed up. That's why the number above only goes up to 12.)

blocks.q: Mika wants the droop gone *fast*, so plans to crank $K_i$ way up. What will happen?

options.text: The droop vanishes quickly and cleanly
options.why: That's the hope. But the pile has momentum: by the time the error reaches zero, it has built up *too much* push.

options.text: The droop vanishes, but the drone wiggles more, and too much makes it shake itself apart
options.why: The pile remembers the past, so it keeps pushing after the drone arrives: overshoot. Too big a $K_i$ and each overshoot is bigger than the last.

options.text: Nothing changes, because $K_i$ only matters at the very end
options.why: The pile starts growing from the first moment there's an error, so $K_i$ shapes the whole flight.

blocks.text: The widget starts at $K_i$ = 10 N/(m·s). Watch three things: the {err|red shaded area} (the error being piled up), the {eff|dashed orange} integral part of the thrust climbing up to the {dis|purple gravity line}, and the droop read-out. Drag $K_i$ to 0 to get Chapter 2's droop back, then try bigger values. $K_p$ is fixed at 20 N/m.

At rest, P and D push nothing (no error, no speed), so the pile holds the whole weight by itself. With $K_i$ = {scrub|ki|eff} N/(m·s), the net {err|red area} must add up to exactly $mg/K_i$ = {calc|area} m·s. Check it against the widget's read-out.
Crank it! $K_i = 50$! Kill it with fire!
…why won't it stop? The bounces grew and grew, and now it's yo-yoing up and down by half a metre, forever!

At 50 you went past some kind of edge. I tried a few values: below about 40 it settles, above it doesn't (and the yo-yo takes about one second per swing). We'll see why in a moment. The pile is *always a little behind*: it keeps pushing up after the drone has passed 2 m.

That's Mika's mistake, and it's a very common one: the integral fixes the droop, but it adds **lag**, and lag makes things swing (the shower taught us that). We need something that pushes back against *speed*.
In Chapter 6 the damper was what calmed the spring down. What if the controller **pretends** to be a damper?
A damper pushes against velocity. So add a term that pushes against how fast the drone is moving:
Look at the drone's equation: drag already gives $-c\,\dot h$. The D term adds $-K_d\,\dot h$ on top, so the drone behaves as if its drag were $c + K_d$. We're adding air resistance **in software**.

With $K_p$ = 20 N/m and $K_d$ = {scrub|kd|eff} N·s/m, the drone feels a drag of {calc|damp|eff} N·s/m, so Chapter 6's damping ratio becomes $\zeta = (c+K_d)/(2\sqrt{m K_p})$ = {calc|zeta}: {calc|regime}. (With I switched on there is a third, slow pole too, so think of this as the personality of the fast pair.)
Strictly, the D in PID is the slope of the *error*, $K_d\,\dot e$. When the setpoint is still, $\dot e = -\dot h$, the same thing. We'll see in a moment why the difference matters.

Flip on **Mika's big I gain** and then add damping. Even $K_d = 0.5$ N·s/m tips it back to stable (it moves the edge out to $K_i = 60$): the endless yo-yo becomes a bounce that dies away. But it still overshoots by at least a quarter, however much D you add. That huge pile simply remembers too much. Now switch Mika's $K_i$ off (back to 10) and try $K_d \approx 3$–5: calm. **I and D trade off**: D buys you room for I, but not unlimited room.
If 4 is good, 10 must be better. Maximum shock absorber!
It creeps up so slowly… and then it goes *past* 2 m anyway? Late?
June, that's your honey drone from Chapter 6 again! Past $K_d \approx 5.3$ the fast pair is overdamped. But now there's a pile too, and a slow drone gives the pile time to overfill.

Critical damping is where ζ = 1: $K_d = 2\sqrt{m K_p} - c \approx 5.3$ N·s/m at $K_p$ = 20. With $K_i$ = 10, going from $K_d$ = 4 to 10 takes the overshoot from 0 to about 8 %, and the settling time from under a second to about 5 s. More D is not always better; the widget now says so when you overdo it.
So D **predicts the future**! It sees where the drone is going and gets there first.

Not really. It only knows the slope *right now*. It's like guessing where a ball will land by assuming it keeps going straight. Usually a decent guess, but it's not magic. Wait until we feed it a jumpy sensor.

sections.title: What each knob does to the poles

blocks.text: Time to use Chapter 8's map. Write the whole loop down, with $\err{e} = \sp{r} - \out{h}$:

blocks.tex: m\ddot{\out h} + c\dot{\out h} = \underbrace{K_p\,\err e + K_i\!\int\!\err e\,dt - K_d\,\dot{\out h}}_{\eff{T}} - \dis{mg}

blocks.text: The integral is awkward, so take the slope of both sides. Slope and area undo each other (Chapter 3), so the slope of $\int \err e\,dt$ is just $\err e$. Gravity is constant, so its slope is **zero**: it simply falls out. With a fixed setpoint, $\dot{\err e} = -\dot{\out h}$. Term by term:

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} \tfrac{d}{dt}\big(K_p\,\err e\big) &= -K_p\,\dot{\out h} \\ \tfrac{d}{dt}\Big(K_i\!\int\!\err e\,dt\Big) &= K_i\,(\sp r - \out h) \\ \tfrac{d}{dt}\big(-K_d\,\dot{\out h}\big) &= -K_d\,\ddot{\out h} \end{aligned}

blocks.text: Put them back together and move everything with $\out h$ to the left. The three dots on $\dddot{\out h}$ mean the slope of the slope of the slope:

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} m\dddot{\out h} + (c + K_d)\,\ddot{\out h} &+ K_p\,\dot{\out h} + K_i\,\out h \\ &= K_i\,\sp r \end{aligned}

blocks.text: Gravity *disappeared* from the equation. That's the droop-killer in algebra form: the final height doesn't care about $mg$ at all.

Guess $e^{st}$ again. **With I active**, the equation is cubic, so there are three poles. If $K_i=0$, there is no integrator: taking the slope added a fake root at $s = 0$, the common factor $s$ cancels, and the PD drone has two poles.

In Chapter 7 a slope became "× s". An area is the opposite, so it becomes "÷ s". Write the controller that way, use the drone's own recipe $P(s) = 1/(ms^2+cs)$ (thrust in, height out), and find the poles as in Chapter 8. Clear the fractions and out comes the same cubic, without taking a single slope:

blocks.tex: \begin{gathered} C(s) = K_p + \frac{K_i}{s} + K_d\,s \\ 1 + C(s)\,\frac{1}{ms^2+cs} = 0 \\ ms^3 + (c+K_d)\,s^2 + K_p\,s + K_i = 0 \end{gathered}

blocks.text: So the ÷ s *is* the extra pole!
And the top of the fraction gets $K_p s + K_i$: a **zero**, at $-K_i/K_p$. (Our D works on $\out h$ only, so it adds no zero.) Keep an eye on it.

For a cubic with all-positive coefficients $a_3 s^3 + a_2 s^2 + a_1 s + a_0$, there's a classic test (the **Routh–Hurwitz** criterion) that says all three poles are in the left half exactly when $a_2 a_1 > a_3 a_0$. For our drone that's the cliff edge:
A rule with two people's names on it. Do we just have to believe it?
Nope. We can find the edge ourselves.

At the instant a wiggly pair reaches the vertical axis, its real part is zero, so try $s=i\omega$ in the cubic. Since $i^2 = -1$ and $i^3 = -i$, the real parts and the sideways parts must each add up to zero:
The second one says $\omega^2 = K_p/m$. Put that into the first:

blocks.title: Why below the line is the safe side

blocks.text: Start with a tiny $K_i$. The PD pair sits safely on the left, and the new pole sits just left of zero, near $-K_i/K_p$. As $K_i$ grows, the poles slide smoothly. To reach the right half, one of them must cross the vertical axis. It can cross at 0 only if $K_i = 0$ (put $s = 0$ into the cubic: only $K_i$ is left), and at $\pm i\omega$ only at the edge we just found. So below the edge, no pole can have crossed.
So the Routh–Hurwitz rule is just "you can't get to the other side without touching the wall".

With $K_p$ = {scrub|kp|eff} N/m and $K_d$ = {scrub|kd|eff} N·s/m, $K_i$ must stay below $(c+K_d)K_p/m$ = {calc|lim} N/(m·s). Right at the edge the drone swings at $\omega = \sqrt{K_p/m}$ = {calc|w} rad/s: one swing every {calc|T} s.

At the starting values ($K_p$ = 20, no D) the edge is 40. That's exactly where Mika's drone went wild, and its yo-yo took about a second per swing: 6.32 rad/s is the P drone's own ωn from Chapter 6. Adding $K_d = 4$ moves the edge out to 200. Don't trust us: change the numbers above, or the sliders below, and watch the poles, the mini-map and the step response.

blocks.title: Why doesn't the slow pole make it slow?

blocks.text: At the start the status says the slowest pole is at −0.54. Chapter 8 said that means about 4/0.54 ≈ 7 s. But the step settles in under 3!
Look for the zero. The I brings one at $-K_i/K_p = -0.5$, right next to that pole. A pole and a zero that close nearly cancel, so that mode hardly shows up when we move the setpoint.
Hardly isn't never. The fast pair alone, with ζ = 0.47, would overshoot about 19 %. The leftover slow mode pushes that to almost 30 %.

items: **The I knob** ($K_i$) brings a third pole into the loop and can push a pair towards the right. Too much and it crosses the line.
**The D knob** ($K_d$) raises the I-gain stability limit by adding damping. Pole paths can turn: more D does not move every pole left.
**The P knob** ($K_p$) mostly spreads the wiggly pair up and down: faster, but more wiggly, unless D keeps up.

blocks.text: Now the real thing: take off from the ground to 2 m with real motors (0–20 N). Earn all four stars. Every time you change a gain, the last flight stays as a faint ghost.
Stuck? Start with $K_d$ around 4 (that's ζ ≈ 0.8, inside Chapter 6's 0.7–1 sweet spot), then raise $K_i$ until the droop goes, then nudge $K_p$.

**Integrator windup:** while the motors are pinned at 20 N, the error pile keeps growing even though the extra push can't happen. Later, all that stored-up push comes out as overshoot. "Anti-windup" simply pauses the pile while the motors are maxed out, and every drone so far in this chapter had it switched on. (A pinned motor has no room left to correct anything, which is why the stars count the time spent pinned.) At $K_p$ = 20, $K_i$ = 20, $K_d$ = 4: about 7 % overshoot with anti-windup, 17 % without. Toggle it and compare.
I switched anti-windup off, set $K_p$ = 30, $K_i$ = 60, $K_d$ = 2… and the drone shot up to 4 m, right out of its picture!
The pile kept growing the whole time the motors were flat out. With anti-windup on, the same gains peak at 2.8 m. Same knobs, very different memory.
Warning 1: the derivative kick

The drone hovers at 1 m. At $t = 1$ s we move the setpoint to 1.5 m. If D uses the slope of the *error*, then the error **jumps** by half a metre in an instant. Its slope is enormous, and so is the push.
A jump of {scrub|dr} m seen through a {scrub|tf} s filter looks like a speed of about {calc|slope} m/s, so with $K_d$ = 4 the D term asks for roughly {calc|spike|eff} N. The motors top out at 20.
On the error it asks for over 200 N? From motors that top out at 20?
And they can't say no politely. They slam flat out for a moment, and the drone gets a kick in the pants.
Taking the slope of the **measured height** instead fixes it: the drone can't teleport, so its height has no jumps. Same damping, no kick. Almost every real PID does this.
Warning 2: noise

Real height sensors jitter by a couple of centimetres. A couple of centimetres of jitter, a thousand times a second, has a **huge slope**. D amplifies it straight into the motors. The fix is to smooth the measurement before taking its slope (a filter with time constant $\tau_f$), at the cost of reacting a bit later.

Read every millisecond, 2 cm of jitter looks like a speed of 20 m/s. Through a filter of $\tau_f$ = {scrub|tf} s, $K_d$ = 4 turns σ = 2 cm of noise into about $K_d\sigma/\tau_f$ = {calc|d|eff} N of thrust jitter; P adds only $K_p\sigma$ = 0.3 N.

The smoothing filter is Newton's cooling rule pointed at the sensor: the smoothed height $h_f$ chases the jittery reading $h_m$ with time constant $\tau_f$, the way the coffee chased room temperature. Fast jitter never gets a chance to move it. Real motion does, about one $\tau_f$ late. That's the price, in seconds.
So the cure for a jumpy D is… a little lag? The same thing that made the pile swing?
About a tenth of a second of it. Lag isn't evil. It's a price, and here it's a cheap one.

Did you spot the drone **drifting upwards** with the short filter? (Watch the average-height read-out.) The chattering thrust gets clipped at 0 N far more often than at 20 N (about 55 % of the time against 5 %: hovering needs only 4.9 N), so the clipped average comes out *above* the weight. Noise plus limits can even move the average. Real hardware is full of surprises like that.
Okay, D does *not* predict the future. It predicts whatever the noise felt like a millisecond ago.

items: **P** pushes in proportion to the error, but must leave a droop to hold the drone up.
**I** piles up past error; the only resting point is zero error, so it kills the droop, which dies with a time constant of about $K_p/K_i$. It adds lag, so too much makes things swing.
**D** pushes against speed: a virtual damper that adds to the drag $c$, so $\zeta = (c+K_d)/(2\sqrt{mK_p})$. More D is not always better: overdamped, the drone creeps and the pile overfills.
The closed loop is $m s^3 + (c + K_d)s^2 + K_p s + K_i$; it's stable exactly when $(c+K_d)K_p > mK_i$.
Take D from the measurement (no kick) and filter it (less noise).

items.q: Which term removes the steady droop under gravity?

options.why: Its pile of error keeps changing until the error is exactly zero, and then it holds the needed 4.9 N by itself.
D reacts to speed. When the drone hovers still, speed is zero and D contributes nothing, so it can't hold anything up.
Bigger $K_p$ shrinks the droop ($mg/K_p$) but never to zero, and it makes the drone wigglier.

items.q: With $K_p = 10$ N/m and $K_d = 1$ N·s/m (drone: $m = 0.5$ kg, $c = 1$ N·s/m), what's the largest $K_i$ before instability?

options.why: Check the formula: $(c + K_d)K_p/m = (1+1)\cdot 10 / 0.5$. You may have forgotten to divide by $m$.
$(1 + 1)\cdot 10 / 0.5 = 40$. Above that, two poles cross into the right half-plane.
Too high. Remember the drag $c$ and the $K_d$ add together first: $(1+1) = 2$, not 4.

items.q: Why take the derivative of the **measurement** rather than of the error?

options.text: When the setpoint jumps, the error jumps too, and its slope is huge: a thrust spike
options.why: Height can't jump, so its slope stays sensible. Same damping, no kick.

options.text: Because the measurement is less noisy than the error
options.why: They have exactly the same noise; the error is setpoint minus measurement.

options.text: It makes the controller more aggressive
options.why: It's the opposite: it removes the aggressive spike on setpoint changes.

items.q: $K_p$ = 20, $K_i$ = 10. Which change makes the take-off overshoot **bigger**?

options.why: Too much damping makes the drone creep, and the pile keeps filling while it creeps: the overshoot goes from 0 % to about 8 %.
That's the good direction: the overshoot drops from about 54 % to 0 %.
A smaller pile remembers less, so it overshoots less (0 % at $K_d$ = 4). It just takes longer to kill the droop.

blocks.text: June tried our drone-style PID on the shower… and it wiggled exactly like we did in Chapter 0. **What is it about delay?**

integral.title: The error pile

status.none: No integral: the drone droops, just like in Chapter 2.
status.slow: The droop is shrinking, but slowly. The pile takes time to build.
status.ringing: Stable, but only just: at 12 s it is still swinging. The closer Ki gets to {lim}, the slower the swings die.
status.gone: Droop gone! The pile now holds up the whole weight.
status.unstable: Past the edge (Ki > {lim}): the bounces grow until the motors hit their limits, and it never settles.

integral.describe: Integral gain {ki}. Droop after 12 seconds: {droop} centimetres.

status.bouncy: Stable, but bouncy. Add more Kd.
status.calm: Calm! The damper soaks up the bounce.
status.tooMuch: More D made it worse! Now it creeps up so slowly that the pile overfills, and it overshoots late. Try less Kd.
status.bigPile: Stable, but Mika's big pile still overshoots by {os} %. No amount of D fixes that: switch Mika's Ki off.

poles.title: Three knobs, three poles
poles.splane: s-plane showing the three closed-loop poles of the drone with PID control

map.aria: Map of Ki against Kd with the stability boundary line; below the line is stable.

poles.stepAria: Step response from 1.5 m to 2 m for the current gains

status.stable: Stable: Ki must stay below {lim}. The slowest pole sits at σ = {s}.
status.unstable: Unstable! Ki is above the edge ({lim}). Two poles crossed into the right half.
status.cancel: (A zero at {z} nearly cancels it, so it barely shows in the step.)

poles.help: The step response starts the drone hovering at 1.5 m and asks for 2 m at t = 1 s, with real 20 N motors (so for big $K_p$ it can differ from the pole picture). Poles beyond the frame become arrows at its edge. ○ is the zero.

playground.title: Tuning playground: take off to 2 m
playground.targets: Stars for: overshoot under {os} %, settling (within 2 %) under {ts} s, no droop (under 1 cm), and motors pinned at a limit for under {sat} s.
playground.allStars: All four stars! That's a real tuning.

hit.back: Bump! It hit what is above it, but the motors keep running, and feedback brings it back to 2 m.
hit.wild: Bump! It hit what is above it. The motors keep running, but with these gains it never settles.

playground.crash: Crash at {t} s! It hit the ground faster than 1.5 m/s, and a crashed drone stays down.

status.error: The error jumps, so its slope is huge: the controller asks for {req} N! The motors can only slam to 20 N. That's a derivative kick.
status.measurement: Height can't jump, so no kick: the most it ever asks for is {req} N, and the climb is smooth.

noise.title: A jittery height sensor

status.chatter: The motors chatter! D is amplifying the noise. Try a longer filter.
status.calm: Much calmer. Of the ±{j} N left, P passes about {p} N straight through; the rest is still D. The price: D now reacts about {tau} s later.
status.noD: No D, nothing to amplify the noise: the ±{j} N left is P passing it straight through. Calm motors, but now only the drag damps the drone.

noise.help: Try $K_d$ = 0: the jitter drops to about 0.3 N (P alone), but then only the drag damps the drone. More D, more noise.
